title: Ninigret, Eastern Niantic Sachem
summary: Ninigret was an Eastern Niantic sachem whose diplomacy reached Rhode Island, New Netherland, and Long Island. His own recorded answers, Montaukett conflict, and survival through King Philip’s War place him within a wider Native political world.
content:
An Eastern Niantic leader across the Sound

Ninigret, also called Janemo, was an Eastern Niantic sachem associated with what is now Rhode Island. Lorén Spears dates his life to about 1610–1677. His diplomacy reached Native communities and colonial governments around Long Island Sound, including the Montauketts, the English colonies, and New Netherland.1 2

His career includes warfare, negotiation, and efforts to preserve his people through the conflicts of the seventeenth century. Reading his own recorded answers alongside accusations made by colonial officials gives a fuller picture than treating him only as Wyandanch’s adversary.1 2

1653: answering accusations about the Dutch

During the Anglo-Dutch conflict, Ninigret’s visit to New Netherland provoked English suspicion. In April 1653, the United Colonies commissioners questioned him about an alleged agreement with the Dutch to attack the English.2

His answers firmly denied such a plan. He distinguished reports of war in Europe from an agreement to fight in New England and challenged the premise that he would endanger his wife, children, relatives, and country in exchange for weapons. He also pointed out that the English lived close to his people, while the Dutch were farther away.2

The commissioners’ record preserves those responses through colonial transcription and interpretation. Even so, it allows readers to hear his stated reasoning instead of accepting the allegation of conspiracy as an established fact.2

1653–1654: Montaukett warfare and the captives

Conflict with Wyandanch brought violence to Montauk. Colonial records describe attacks and captives, including the daughter later known as Quashawam. The conflict involved Native rivalries and the military protection claimed by the English colonies.2 3

Thomas James’s letter to John Winthrop Jr. of September 6, 1654 reports an urgent effort to forward ransom that had been delayed through Thomas Stanton. Gardiner’s later account also described his assistance in recovering captives. These records connect Ninigret’s war with the family history of Montaukett leadership.2 3

In 1654 the United Colonies ordered an armed intervention under Major Simon Willard, coupled with demands concerning Pequots living under Ninigret’s authority. The proceedings placed several Native communities within a struggle over tribute, jurisdiction, and who could claim protection over whom.2 3

1656: disputed charges against Wyandanch

The commissioners again dealt with the two leaders in 1656. Ninigret’s allegations involved a supposed plot to poison the Mohegan sachem Uncas. Wyandanch appeared with supporters; the commissioners did not receive the proof needed to sustain the accusation.2

The hearing shows how Native rivalries were also fought through colonial councils and legal accusations. Its outcome should not be converted into evidence that a poisoning plot actually existed.2

1669: tribute claims and a Montaukett answer

Ninigret’s Rhode Island testimony in July 1669 stated that Wyandanch’s daughter was dead and asserted claims over the Montauketts. On November 3, Checkannoo and other Montaukett leaders formally rejected the claimed submission and declared that further tribute required the New York governor’s approval.4

That collective answer, reproduced by Tooker, places Cockenoe and the remaining Montaukett leadership in the story. Ninigret’s claims were contested by the people they concerned.4

Survival through King Philip’s War

Ninigret stayed out of King Philip’s War in 1675–1676 and died in 1677. Spears’s account places his life within the continuing history of Niantic and Narragansett people, whose communities survived the war’s devastating consequences.1

The sea between Rhode Island and Long Island connected these histories. Ninigret’s biography opens that wider setting: diplomacy, refuge, coercion, kinship, and competing claims to Native political independence.1

  2. United Colonies records: Wyandanch diplomacy, 1644–1657. David Pulsifer, ed., Records of the Colony of New Plymouth, vols. IX–X (1859): IX, pp. 18–19 (1644 certificate); X, pp. 9–11 (Ninigret’s 1653 answers), 96–98 (1653 Montauk conflict), 125–134 (1654 intervention), 169–172 (1656 hearing).
  3. Thomas James to John Winthrop Jr., September 6, 1654. Thomas James to John Winthrop Jr., East Hampton, September 6, 1654; Massachusetts Historical Society Collections, 4th series, VII, p. 482; transcribed in Curtiss C. Gardiner, Lion Gardiner and His Descendants (1890), p. 63.
  4. Cockenoe-de-Long Island: documentary biography. why_this_matters: Ninigret's story shows that Native Long Island history was never isolated from the wider Native Northeast. His actions across Long Island Sound affected Montaukett leadership, Quashawam's life, and the diplomacy and violence surrounding seventeenth-century Native communities.
activity_update_summary: Expanded historical context, family and land connections, linked references, and dated Historic Moments.
